title: The Ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
hook: he goes up and two men ask why they're staring at the sky

segments.voice: Yesterday, breakfast on the beach, and three questions by a charcoal fire. Your line was thou knowest that I love thee. Each answer came back with a job.

You've dropped someone at the airport. You've hugged, they've gone through security, and you're at the big window watching planes take off, not even sure which one is theirs. You keep looking anyway. Eventually somebody taps you on the shoulder: time to go. For forty days after Easter, Luke says, the risen Jesus kept appearing to his friends. Then, on a hill called Olivet, just outside Jerusalem, it ends. He's lifted up, a cloud takes him out of their sight, and they stand there, eleven grown men, staring at the sky.
screen: `STARING THROUGH THE AIRPORT WINDOW.` → `FORTY DAYS OF APPEARANCES.` → `A CLOUD TAKES HIM.`

segments.voice: Just before, they ask a question that shows they still don't quite get it: "Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" Is it now? He doesn't answer the when. He gives them a job: they'll receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on them, and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, and Judea, and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he goes up. While they're still looking, two men in white stand beside them and say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" He'll come back, they say, the same way you saw him go. Ascension comes from the Latin for going up, climbing. But Catholics don't hear it as Jesus leaving the building. The Church teaches that he takes our human nature, wounds and all, into the life of God, and where he's gone, Catholics hope to follow. The angels' question isn't a scolding, it's a nudge: stop staring, you've got a job. So they walk back to Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's walk, to an upstairs room, and pray together, with Mary his mother among them, for about nine days. Catholic tradition calls this wait the first novena, from the Latin novem, nine: nine days of prayer. Catholics keep the feast forty days after Easter, a Thursday, though in many places it's moved to the following Sunday.
screen: `IS IT NOW? WRONG QUESTION.` · `WITNESSES, TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `OUR NATURE TAKEN INTO GOD.` · `NINE DAYS: THE FIRST NOVENA.` · then, large: `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP TO HEAVEN?`

segments.voice: If you can, look at the sky for a moment, or picture it, and let yourself hope, or wonder, or pray, whatever is honest. Then bring your eyes back down to the room, think of one thing you've been putting off that would help someone, and picture yourself starting it. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Ascension. From the Latin for going up. Forty days after Easter, Jesus is taken up, and his friends are sent back down the hill to work. Today's word.
Your line: why stand you looking up. There's work to do down here. That's day seventy-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter (in many dioceses on the following Sunday), and many pray a novena, nine days of prayer, from the Ascension to Pentecost.

original.note: Latin: a going up, a climbing. from ascendere, to climb.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus floated away into space.
what it means: the Church says he takes our human nature into the life of God, and sends his friends back to work.
what a scholar hears: Luke tells it twice, at the end of his Gospel and the start of Acts, as a hinge between the two books. and the first novena is the nine days that follow.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 1:6 and 1:11 given from memory; confirm.
The Ascension took place from Mount Olivet (Acts 1:12); Luke 24:50 says near Bethany. Script says 'a hill called Olivet'.
Novena origin: the nine days between Ascension and Pentecost are traditionally called the first novena. 'About nine days' allows for counting. Confirm phrasing.
Ascension Thursday transferred to the Seventh Sunday of Easter in most US ecclesiastical provinces and many countries. Confirm.
Ecclesiastical Latin pronunciation of ascensio given as ah-SHEN-see-oh. Confirm.

Audit (second sample): the teach said the word novena 'comes from' this wait; the word comes from Latin novem (nine), and the wait is what tradition calls the first novena. Fixed. The hook's 'you can't park here' (said at an indoor window) was replaced.
